ROM Motion Tracking Rules
AI-Based Rules for Tracking Body Movement in Telehealth PT
1. General Guidelines for AI-Based ROM Tracking
Tracking Method: Use computer vision (e.g., OpenPose, MediaPipe) or IMU sensors to track joint angles in real-time.
Reference Points: Use bony landmarks as tracking points (e.g., acromion for the shoulder, greater trochanter for the hip).
Axis of Movement: Define movement planes (sagittal, frontal, transverse) and track joint angles relative to anatomical neutral (0°).
Compensation Detection: Identify abnormal movement patterns (e.g., lumbar extension during shoulder flexion).
Side Comparisons: Bilateral symmetry should be analyzed for injury detection.
2. Joint-Specific ROM Guidelines
Cervical Spine (Neck)
Flexion: Normal ROM 45–50° (Limited = stiffness, Excessive = hypermobility)
Extension: Normal ROM 45–75° (Pain = instability)
Lateral Flexion (Side-bending): Normal ROM 40–45° (Asymmetry = muscle imbalance)
Rotation: Normal ROM 70–90° (Reduced = cervical radiculopathy)
Shoulder
Flexion: Normal ROM 160–180° (Compensation: lumbar extension)
Extension: Normal ROM 45–60° (Limited = frozen shoulder)
Abduction: Normal ROM 160–180° (Abnormal: scapular winging)
External Rotation: Normal ROM 80–90° (Limited = rotator cuff tear)
Internal Rotation: Normal ROM 60–100° (Reduced = GIRD in athletes)
Elbow
Flexion: Normal ROM 140–150° (Limited = post-surgical stiffness)
Extension: Normal ROM 0–5° (Hyperextension = ligament laxity)
Supination: Normal ROM 80–90° (Limited = radial-ulnar joint dysfunction)
Pronation: Normal ROM 80–90° (Pain = medial elbow instability)
Wrist
Flexion: Normal ROM 70–90° (Limited = carpal instability)
Extension: Normal ROM 70–90° (Excessive = gymnast wrist instability)
Radial Deviation: Normal ROM 20–25° (Pain = scaphoid injury)
Ulnar Deviation: Normal ROM 30–40° (Reduced = post-trauma stiffness)
Thoracic Spine
Flexion: Normal ROM 20–45° (Excessive = kyphosis)
Extension: Normal ROM 15–25° (Limited = ankylosing spondylitis)
Rotation: Normal ROM 30–35° (Asymmetry = scoliosis)
Lateral Flexion: Normal ROM 25–30° (Limited = thoracic stiffness)
Lumbar Spine (Lower Back)
Flexion: Normal ROM 40–60° (Excessive = disc herniation risk)
Extension: Normal ROM 20–35° (Excessive = facet joint syndrome)
Lateral Flexion: Normal ROM 15–25° (Limited in unilateral back pain)
Rotation: Normal ROM 3–18° (Reduced in chronic lower back pain)
Hip
Flexion: Normal ROM 110–125° (Pain = hip impingement)
Extension: Normal ROM 10–20° (Limited = hip contracture)
Abduction: Normal ROM 40–50° (Asymmetry = hip instability)
Adduction: Normal ROM 20–30° (Reduced = hip arthritis)
Internal Rotation: Normal ROM 30–40° (Limited in FAI syndrome)
External Rotation: Normal ROM 40–60° (Excessive = hypermobility)
Knee
Flexion: Normal ROM 130–150° (Limited = post-surgical stiffness)
Extension: Normal ROM 0–5° (Hyperextension = ACL laxity)
Internal Rotation: Normal ROM 10–15° (Limited = meniscus tears)
External Rotation: Normal ROM 30–40° (Pain = IT band syndrome)
Ankle
Dorsiflexion: Normal ROM 10–20° (Limited = Achilles tightness)
Plantarflexion: Normal ROM 40–50° (Pain = posterior impingement)
Inversion: Normal ROM 30–35° (Limited in ankle sprains)
Eversion: Normal ROM 15–20° (Reduced in peroneal tendon dysfunction)
3. AI-Based Compensation Detection Rules
Shoulder Flexion Compensation:
Normal: Scapula moves after 90° flexion.
Abnormal: Early excessive scapular elevation = rotator cuff weakness.
Lumbar Flexion in Squatting:
Normal: Hip moves first, then lumbar spine.
Abnormal: Early lumbar rounding = weak core or tight hamstrings.
Knee Valgus in Squats/Lunges:
Normal: Knees aligned with toes.
Abnormal: Medial knee collapse = weak glute medius (ACL risk).
Gait Analysis (Walking Pattern):
Normal: Symmetric step length and cadence.
Abnormal: Limping, excessive hip drop (Trendelenburg sign).


Knee Pain Compensation Detection Rules

Hip Hike: Excessive elevation of the pelvis on the affected side to compensate for knee stiffness.
Foot Dragging: Decreased dorsiflexion due to knee pain.
Circumduction: Outward swinging of the leg to avoid bending the knee.
Decreased Step Length: Shorter step on the affected side.
Increased Hip External Rotation: Attempting to offload knee flexion stress.

Reduced Knee Flexion: Inability to reach normal depth (~90 degrees).
Forward Trunk Lean: Increased hip flexion to reduce knee demand.

Tennis Elbow (Lateral Epicondylitis) Compensation Detection Rules
1. Wrist & Forearm Motion Analysis
Reduced Wrist Extension Strength: Weakness in wrist extensors.
Overuse of Finger Flexors: Excessive grip strength instead of wrist stabilization.
Excessive Wrist Flexion with Gripping: To avoid engaging wrist extensors.
2. Shoulder & Elbow Movement Patterns
Increased Shoulder Abduction: Lifting the arm excessively to compensate for weak forearm muscles.
Reduced Elbow Extension During Activities: Avoiding full extension due to pain.
Overuse of Upper Trapezius: Shrugging shoulder while gripping or lifting objects.
3. Asymmetrical Force Application
Uneven Distribution of Grip Strength: More force applied on the non-affected hand.
Compensatory Finger Activation: Using more finger flexors instead of wrist extensors.
4. Common Movement Compensations
Excessive Forearm Supination: Avoidance of painful pronation.
Avoidance of Repetitive Wrist Extension Movements: Especially in typing, lifting, and gripping.
Back Pain (Lumbar and Thoracic) Compensation Detection Rules
1. Gait & Postural Deviations
Antalgic Gait: Shorter stride to avoid lumbar compression.
Increased Pelvic Tilt: Excessive anterior tilt (lordosis) or posterior tilt (flat back) to reduce pain.
Reduced Spinal Rotation: Avoiding twisting due to pain.
2. Lifting & Bending Movements
Excessive Knee Bending Instead of Hip Hinge: Using the knees more than necessary to avoid lumbar stress.
Rounded Back While Bending: Increased thoracic flexion due to lumbar instability.
Asymmetric Weight Shifting: Leaning to one side to unload pain.
3. Sitting Posture & Ergonomics
Forward Head Posture: Common in chronic back pain sufferers.
Increased Thoracic Kyphosis: Rounded upper back due to compensatory movement.
Excessive Reliance on Armrests: Reducing spinal engagement by supporting weight with arms.
4. Core & Hip Stability Analysis
Decreased Glute Activation: Avoiding hip engagement in movements like bridges or squats.
Excessive Hip Flexor Activation: Overuse of iliopsoas to stabilize the spine.
Increased Paraspinal Muscle Stiffness: Over-recruitment of spinal erectors.
5. Breathing Patterns
Shallow Chest Breathing: Instead of using the diaphragm.
Overuse of Neck Muscles: Using SCM and scalene muscles for breathing instead of deep core engagement.
How AI Can Track and Detect Compensations
Computer Vision & Pose Estimation: Detects deviations from ideal movement patterns.
Wearable Sensors (IMUs): Captures ROM and joint angles dynamically.
Pressure Sensors: Analyzes weight distribution in foot and hand pressure.
Electromyography (EMG) Sensors: Measures muscle activation patterns for compensations.

Osteokinematics
The  tibiofemoral  joint  is  a  double  condyloid  joint   with 2 degrees of freedom. Flexion–extension occurs in the sagit- tal plane around a medial–lateral axis and rotation occurs in the transverse plane around a vertical (longitudinal) axis.1  The incongruence and asymmetry of the tibiofemoral joint surfaces combined  with  muscle  activity  and  ligamentous  restraints produce  an  automatic  rotation.  This  automatic  rotation  is involuntary and occurs primarily toward the end of extension when motion stops on the shorter lateral femoral condyle but continues on the longer medial condylar surface. During the last portion of the active extension range of motion (ROM)

automatic rotation produces what is referred to as the screw- home mechanism, or “locking,” of the knee. For example, during non-weight-bearing active knee extension with the tibia moving on the femur, the tibia laterally rotates during the last 10 to 15 degrees of extension to lock the knee.2  Therefore, in the fully extended position of the knee, the tibia is laterally rotated in relation to the femur. To unlock the knee, either the tibia has to rotate medially or the femur has to rotate laterally.
This automatic rotation is not under voluntary control and should not be confused with the voluntary rotation that is possible when the knee is flexed. At 90 degrees of flexion the greatest range of tibial rotation is possible.3,4  In a study by Almquistand colleagues of 120 healthy individuals (60 males and 60 females), about 40% of the total voluntary knee rota- tion  was  estimated  as  being  internal  rotation  and  60%  as external rotation.5
Arthrokinematics
In  non-weight-bearing  active  motion,  the  concave  tibial articulating surfaces slide on the convex femoral condyles in the same direction as the movement of the shaft of the tibia. The tibial condyles slide posteriorly on the femoral condyles during flexion and the tibial condyles slide anteriorly on the femoral condyles during extension.
In a weight-bearing situation the larger articulating sur- faces of the convex femoral condyles must roll and slide in opposite directions to remain on the smaller tibial surfaces. During  weight-bearing  flexion,  the  femoral  condyles  roll posteriorly and slide anteriorly. The menisci follow the roll of the condyles by distorting posteriorly in flexion. In exten- sion, the femoral condyles roll anteriorly and slide poste- riorly.1  In the last portion of extension, motion stops at the lateral femoral condyle, but sliding continues on the medial femoral condyleto produce locking of the knee.
The patella slides superiorly in extension and inferiorly in flexion. Some patellar rotation and tilting accompany the sliding during flexion and extension.
Capsular Pattern
The capsular pattern at the knee is characterized by a smaller limitation of extension than of flexion and no restriction of rotations.6,7   Fritz and associates8   found that patients with  a capsular pattern, defined as a ratio of extension loss to flex- ion loss between 0.03 and 0.50, were 3.2 times more likely to have arthritis or arthroses of the knee.

KNEE EXTENSORS
The major knee extensor is the quadriceps femoris,
which consists of the following four muscles: rectus
femoris, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, and vastus
intermedius. The rectus femoris is the only one of the four muscles that crosses both the hip and the knee
joints. It arises proximally from two tendons: an ante-   rior tendon from the anterior inferior iliac spine and a  posterior tendon from a groove superior to the brim    of the acetabulum. The three vastus muscles originate on the femur and merge with the rectus femoris in
a thick, ﬂat common tendon called the quadriceps
tendon, which inserts into the proximal aspect of the   patella. The quadriceps tendon continues distally over the patella to attach to the apex of the patella. The
part of the quadriceps tendon that continues distal to the patella to attach to the tibial tuberosity is known   as the patella tendon or ligament (Fig. 9.9).

sively moves into ﬂexion to accommodate the shortened muscle. The three vastus muscles also produce active

The distal hamstring length test or hamstring passive knee extension (PKE) test is also called the popliteal  angle (PA) test because the angle that is being mea-  sured is the popliteal angle between the femur and   the lower leg.
Testing Position
Position the individual supine with the hip on the side   being tested in 90 degrees of ﬂexion and 0 degrees of abduction, adduction, and rotation (Fig. 9.15). Initially,  the knee being tested is allowed to relax in ﬂexion.
The lower extremity that is not being tested rests
on the examining table with the knee fully extended   and the hip in 0 degrees of ﬂexion, extension, abduc- tion, adduction, and rotation.
Stabilization
Stabilize the femur to prevent rotation, abduction,  and adduction at the hip and to maintain the hip in 90 degrees of ﬂexion.



Testing Motion
Extend the knee to the end of the ROM. The end     of the testing motion occurs when resistance is felt  from tension in the posterior thigh and further knee extension causes the hip to move toward extension (Figs. 9.16 and 9.17).
Normal End-Feel
The end-feel is ﬁrmowing to tension in the semi-    membranosus, semitendinosus, and biceps femoris muscles.
Goniometer Alignment
See Figure 9.18.
1. Center fulcrum of the goniometer over the lateral epicondyle of the femur.
2. Align proximal arm with the lateral midline of the   femur, using the greater trochanter for a reference.
3. Align distal arm with the lateral midline of the ﬁb-  ula, using the lateral malleolus and ﬁbular head for reference.

Gender
In general,it appears that females have greater knee ROM and more knee joint laxity than their male counterparts. Soucie and colleagues32  found that in addition to age differences, the following gender difference was present: Females had greater

joint mobility in all age-groups in nearly all joints compared with males. The authors also found some evidence to support the finding that the joint mobility index increases in females after they enter puberty.
Beighton, Solomon, and Soskolne29   defined more than 10 degrees of knee extension beyond 0 as hyperextension and included this criterion in a study of joint laxity in 1,081 males and females. Females in the study had more joint laxity than males at any age. Loudon, Goist, and Loudon41  operationally defined knee hyperextension (genurecurvatum) as more than 5 degrees of extension beyond the 0 position. Clinically, the authors had observed that not only was hyperextension more common in females than in males, but also that the condi- tion might be associated with functional deficits in muscle strength, instability, and poor proprioceptive control of ter- minal knee extension. The authors cautioned that the female athlete with hyperextended knees may be at risk for anterior cruciate ligament injury. Hall and colleagues42  found that 10 female patients diagnosed with hypermobility syndrome had alterations in proprioceptive acuity at the knee compared with an age-matched and gender-matched control group.
Almquist  and  colleagues5    measured  knee  rotation  in 60 healthy women and 60 healthy male volunteers aged 15 to  older than  60 years. Measurements  of total knee rota- tion were taken in both knees at 90, 60, and 30 degrees of knee flexion using applied torques of 6 and 9 Nm (newton meters). No significant differences were found in the total internal–external ROM between the right and left knees at any age or gender. However, the women in the study showed a significantly larger knee rotation ROM than the men at all tested degrees of knee flexion and at all applied torques. The women had a 10% to 20% larger range of total knee rotation than did the men.
James and Parker43  studied knee flexion ROM in 80 men and women who ranged in age from 70 years to older than 85 years. Women had greater ROM in both active and pas- sive  knee  flexion  than  men.  Overall,  knee  flexion  values were lower than expected for both genders, possibly owing to the fact that subjects were measured in the prone position, where the two-joint rectus femoris muscle may have limited the ROM.
In contrast to the findings of James and Parker,43 Escalante and coworkers38  found that female subjects had reduced pas- sive knee flexion ROM compared with males of the same age. However, the women had on average only 2 degrees less knee flexion than did the men. The women also had a higher body mass index than did the men, which may have contributed to their reduced knee flexion.
Schwarze and Denton25  observed no differences owing to gender in a study of 527 girls and 473 boys aged 1 to 3 days. However, it is possible that at this early stage of development gender differences had not yet had time to become manifest. Conversely, Cleffken and colleagues44  also found no gender differences in active and passive knee flexion and extension ROM in 23 male and 19 female healthy volunteers aged 19 to 27 years.

Body Mass Index
Body mass index (BMI) is a simple index of weight-for- height that is used to classify overweight and obesity in both male and female adults. It is defined as a person’s weight  in  kilograms  divided  by  the  square  of  height  in meters (kg/m2). According to the mostrecent fact sheet by the World Health Organization (WHO), a person is over- weight if he or she has a BMI greater than or equal to 25. If the person has a BMI greater than or equal to 30, then that person is considered obese.45  Lichtenstein and associates46  found that among 647 community-dwelling elderly subjects (aged 64 to 78 years), those with high BMI had lower knee ROM than did their counterparts with low BMI. Functional Range of Motion
Walking, going up and down  stairs,  and various activities of daily living such as getting up and sitting down, getting in and out of a bath, squatting, and kneeling are included in the following section. Walking appears to require the least knee ROM, whereas going up and downstairs, getting in and out of a chair and a bath, kneeling, and squatting require the most ROM.
Table 9.5 provides knee ROM values required for vari- ous functional activities including gait and going up and down stairs. Figures 9.19 to 9.21 show functional activities requir- ing different amounts of knee flexion. Of the activities mea- sured by Jevsevar and coworkers60  (stair ascent and descent, gait,and rising from a chair), stair ascent required the greatest range of knee motion.
Oberg,Karsznia, and Oberg61  used electrogoniometers to measure knee joint motion in midstance and swing phases of gait in 233 healthy males and females aged 10 to 79 years. Only minor changes were attributable to age, and the authors determined that an increase in knee angle of about 0.5 degrees per decade occurred at midstance and a decrease of 0.5 to 0.8 degrees in knee angle occurred in the swing phase.
Rowe and associates62   found that walking required the least amount of knee flexion for the 20 elderly subjects (aged 54 to 90 years) in their study, whereas getting in and out of a bath required the most knee flexion (135 degrees). The authors suggested that a clinical guideline of at least 110 degrees of flexionis necessary to allow patients to be able to walk, nego- tiate stairs, and get in and out of chairs. A goal of 90 degrees of knee flexionis not adequate to allow patients to carry out normal activities.

Reliability and Validity of Range of Motion Measurement
Reliability studies of active and passive range of knee motion have been conducted in healthy subjects74–79   and in patient populations. Similar to findings at other joints, the results of knee studies show that usually intratester reliability is higher than intertester reliability. Reliability and ROM values also appear to be affected by measurement instruments and testing positions and by the type of motion (active or passive) tested. Factors that have been shown to improve reliability include training of testers, marking of landmarks, careful patient posi- tioning, use of more than one person to assist with stabiliza- tion (especially in the presence of spasticity), and assistance in holding of heavy extremities.

Reliability of the Universal Goniometer in Healthy Populations
Boone and associates74  had four testers use universal goniom- eters (UG) to measure active knee flexion and extension ROM at four weekly sessions. Intratester reliability was higher than intertester reliability, and the total intratester SD for measure- ments at the knee was 4 degrees, whereas the intertester SD was 5.9 degrees. The authors recommended that when more than one tester measures the range of knee motion, changes in ROM should exceed 6 degrees to show that a real change has occurred.
Rheault and coworkers76  found good intertester reliabil- ity for the UG (Table 9.6) and the fluid-based inclinometer (r = 0.83) for measurements of active knee flexion. How- ever, significant differences in the ROM values were found between the instruments. Therefore, the authors concluded that although the universal and fluid-based goniometers each appeared to have good reliability, they should not be used interchangeably in the clinical setting.


Bartholomy, Chandler, and Kaplan77  had similar find- ings. These authors compared measurements of passive knee flexion ROM taken with a UG with measurements taken with a fluid-based inclinometer and an Optotrak motion- analysis system. Eighty healthy subjects aged 22 to 43 years were measured. Individually, the UG and the inclinometer were found to be reliable instruments for measuring passive knee flexion. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) for the UG were 0.97, and ICCs for the fluid inclinometer were 0.98.  However,  there  were  significant  differences  in  the ROM values obtained among the three devices used, and the authors caution that these instruments should not be used interchangeably.
Mollinger and Steffan35   collected intratester reliabil- ity data on measurement of knee extension made by two testers using a UG. Intraclass correlation coefficients for repeated measurements of knee extension were high (see Table 9.6), with differences between measurements aver- aging 1 degree.

Reliability of the Universal Goniometer in Patient Populations
Rothstein,  Miller,  and  Roettger80    investigated   intratester, intertester,  and  interdevice  reliability  in  a  study  involving 12 patients referred to physical therapy for knee problems. Intratester reliability for passive ROM measurements for knee flexion and extension was high. Intertester reliability also was high among the  12 testers for passive ROM measurements for flexion but was lower for knee extension measurements (see Table 9.6). Intertester reliability was not improved by repeated measurements but was improved when testers used the same patient positioning. Interdevice reliability was high for  all  measurements. Neither the  composition  of the  UG (metal or plastic) nor the size (large or small) had a significant effect on the measurements.
Watkins and associates81  compared passive ROM mea- surements of the knees of 43 patients made by 14 physical therapists who used a UG and VE. These authors found that intratester reliability with the UG was high for both knee flexion and knee extension. Intertester reliability for gonio- metric measurements also was high for knee flexion but only good for knee extension (see Table 9.6). Both intratester and intertester reliability were lower for VE than for goniometric

measurement. The authors suggested that therapists should not substitute VEs for goniometric measurements when assessing a patient’s range of knee motion because of the additional error that is introduced with use of visual estimation.
Pandya  and  colleagues82    studied  intratester  and  inter- tester  reliability  of  passive  knee  extension  measurements in  150 children aged  1 to 20 years who had a diagnosis of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Intratester reliability with use of the UG was high, but intertester reliability was only fair (see Table 9.6).
McWhirk and Glanzman83   had  two physical therapists measure the knee ROM and the popliteal angle in 46 knees in 25 children (aged 2 to 18 years) with spastic cerebral palsy. The intertester reliability  of knee  extension  measurements was an ICC of 0.78 with a 95% confidence interval (CI) = ±1.75, and the popliteal angle measurement had an ICC of 0.93 with a 95% CI = ±1.47. The therapists helped each other during the measurements by having one or the other either provide support for the test leg or stabilize the other extremity.
In a study by Lessen and associates,84  two physical thera- pists used a long-arm UG to measure active and passive knee flexion and extension in 30 patients within the first 4 days after total knee arthoplasty. Measurements were taken with the patients supine in a hospital bed and in the sitting posi- tion on an examination table. The highest levels of agreement between the testers were found for passive flexion and exten- sion in the sitting position. The lowest level of agreement was found for passive flexion in the supine position with 16.2 to 19.0 degrees difference between the two testers. Intraclass correlation coefficient values for intertester reliability were highest for active and passive flexion while sitting.
Kilgour, McNair, and Stott85  had three pediatric physi- cal therapists measure bilateral knee extension in 25 children with spastic cerebral palsy ranging in age from 6 to 17 years and 25 age- and sex-matched controls. Intrasessional absolute differences ranged from 0 to 2.7 degrees in the control group and 0 to 2.4 degrees in the cerebral palsy (CP) group. Intrases- sionalICCs were good in the control group (ICC = 0.79–0.87) and excellent in the CP group (ICC = 0.97–0.99). Interses- sional ICCs were lower for both the control and CP groups, but only the control group had unacceptable ICCs (0.34–0.67) compared with an ICC of 0.89 to 0.92 for the CP group. The authors concluded that sagittal plane ROM measures have similar levels of reliability in children with spastic CP com- pared with healthy controls both within and between sessions.

Reliability of the Electronic Digital Inclinometer and Electrogoniometer
Cleffken and associates44 conducted a study to determine both intratester and intertester reproducibility for measurements of active and passive knee flexion and extension in 42 healthy male volunteers. Each motion was measured by two testers three times in four measurement sessions using the CYBEX ED1320, an electronic digital inclinometer. Measurements of passive maximum flexion of the knee resulted in a smaller detectable difference than active knee flexion for intertester comparisons. Intratester reliability showed better reproduc- ibility with SDDs reduced by 0.4 to 1.9 degrees over inter- tester values.
Piriyaprasarth and colleagues87  assessed intratester and intertester reliability of knee measurements using a flexi- ble electrogoniometer at two different fixed flexion angles (45 and 75 degrees) in sitting, supine, and standing positions. Thirty-seven healthy adults (mean age 31 years) participated in the intratester study, and 35 healthy adults (mean age 30 years) participated in the intertester reliability study. Ten repetitions of joint angles were taken by two testers. Intratester reliability of measurements ranged from fair for supine (ICC = 0.75–0.76), to good in sitting (ICC = 0.86–0.87), and in standing (ICC = 0.87–0.88). Intertester reliability was poor to fair for supine (ICC = 0.58–0.71), and for sitting (ICC = 0.68–0.79),and poor to good for standing (ICC = 0.57–0.80). The sitting position had higher ICCs and lower standard errors of measurement (SEMs) for both intratester and intertester reliability compared with the supine position. The SEM for repeated measures for the same tester was less than 1.7 degrees when the same tester repeated the measurements. One drawback of the study was that only angles less than 90 degrees were measured.
Reliability and Validity of Digital Imaging and Photography
Bennett  and  colleagues88    recorded  four  digital  images  of each of 10 subjects’ limbs in the following four positions: active extension, passive maximum extension, active flex- ion, and passive maximum flexion. A physical therapist and an orthopedic registrar independently measured each of the 40 images for interobserver reliability and the results were analyzed using Pearson product moment correlation coeffi- cients (r = 0.993 – 0.995). Intraclass correlation coefficients


ranged from 0.91 to 0.99 with SDs of 0.9 to  1.9 degrees. According to the authors, the advantages of using this tech- nique are that it does not rely on skin marks over bony land- marks, which are often only visualized and not marked. It also eliminates the need for therepositioning of the goniom- eter andrepalpation of bony landmarks that may be required when the overlying skin moves and alters the marking of the bony landmarks. Another advantage is that serial digital images can be made and rechecked. The major disadvantage is that it is relatively time consuming and both examiners were measuring from the same photograph, which isnottyp- ical in a clinical setting.

For both methods, intraobserver reliability for extension was lower compared with flexion. Intraobserver SEM of the digital method was smaller than the UG method. The authors concluded that measuring maximum flexion and extension on digital photographs was more reli- able than standard goniometry.

A secondary objective was to compare ROM values obtained with the 3D Vicon motion-analysis program. Twenty-six healthy individ- uals aged 21 to 26 years participated in the study. Reliability of measurement ranged from 0.62 to 0.88 for the motion- analysis system and from 0.79 to 0.098 for the app. The MDC

Reliability of the Rotameter and Rottameter
A limited number of studies and instruments exist to measure voluntary knee rotation. Tsai and colleagues15  at the Univer- sity of Pittsburgh developed a device called the Rotameter to measure passive internal and external rotation at the knee. The device consists of a foam walker boot with a force/moment sensor affixed to the sole of the boot, which is used in con- junction with a magnetic tracking system. The device was tested on 11 subjects. Intratester reliability within one testing session with knee angles of 30 and 90 degrees of knee flexion found that the ICCs were both greater than 0.95 with associ- ated SEMs less than 1 degree and a 95% confidence inter- valless than 2.0 degrees. Intertester reliability at 90 degrees of flexion had  average  ICCs  and  SEMs  of 0.88  and  1.6, respectively.
Almquist and colleagues16  examined the within-day and 1 week apart intratester reliability of an external device called the Rottameter. The ICCs ranged from 0.50 to 0.94 at all three flexion angles (90, 60, and 30 degrees) with 6 and 9 Nm of applied torque. A physiotherapist measured both knees in 10 healthy adults (6 females and 4 males), once in the morn- ing and once in the afternoon of the same day. Another group of 10 females and males were tested 1 week apart at the same time of day. The highest within-day ICC was calculated at 0.94 Nm of applied torque at a 30-degree flexion angle. Intert- ester reliability was measured by two independent physiother- apists and the highest ICC was 0.87 at 90 degrees and 0.61 to 0.70 at 30 degrees at 6 Nm of applied torque. The Rottame- ter was judged by the authors to be a good (ICC = 0.75) to excellent (ICC above 0.75) device concerning reliability for measuring knee rotation with 6 and 9 Nm of applied torque at the three knee angles. The ROM for total rotations at 9 Nm of applied torque was 70 degrees to 79 degrees as measured by the Rottameter. The main drawback of this device is that it is not easily transported because it is a heavy wooden box-like structure and is a prototype.

Reliability and Validity of Smartphone Applications
Jenny92    used  a  smartphone  application  to  measure  knee flexion angles taken during 10 total knee arthroplasties that were being performed on 4 men and 6 women (mean age of

69 years) with end-stage knee osteoarthritis. The smartphone was encased in a sterile plastic bag and placed as follows: one on the anterior surface of the thigh proximal to the skin incision and the other on the anterior surface of the distal tibia slightly distal to the incision. The knee was positioned according to the navigated system at six positions starting at full extension and ending at maximal flexion. Therefore, six navigated and six smartphone measurements were obtained for each patient giving a total of 60 navigated and 60 smartphone measure- ments. Results showed that there was a significant correla- tion between the navigated and smartphone measurements of all individual patients (r2  = 0.88–0.99) that were operated on and the mean paired difference between the application and the navigation system was not significant (−1.1 degrees, ±6.8 degrees). Results showed that the coherence between both measurements was good. See Table 9.7.
Ockendon and Gilbert93   compared a smartphone accel- erometer-based knee goniometer with a long-armed conven- tional goniometer for the assessment of a fixed knee deformity. Five healthy males aged 30 to 40 years were studied. The smartphone goniometer had an intraobserver correlation of r = 0.98 compared with r = 0.95 for the UG. The smartphone goniometer had an interobserver correlation of r = 0.98 com- pared with r = 0.93 for the UG. The authors concluded that the smartphone goniometer is a reliable device for measurement of knee flexion in the clinic.
Ferriereo and colleagues94   assessed  the reliability  of a smartphone-based  application  (Dr.  Goniometer)  developed for photographic-based goniometry by comparing the smart- phone application’s measurements of knee joint angles with measurements taken with a UG. In Part I, four raters per- formed repeated measurements with both the smartphone app and the UG at different fixed knee angles. The intrarater ICC was 0.95 and the interrater ICC was 0.99. In Part II, 10 other raters measured photographs of the knee at different flex- ion angles ranging from 20 to  145 degrees on a battery of 35 photographs. The results showed that inter- and intrarater correlations were always more than 0.96. However, according to the authors both UG and photographic angle goniometry are more reliable with greater degrees of knee flexion. Agree- ment between Dr. Goniometer and the UG showed a width of 18.2 degrees (95% limits of agreement [LOA]) (LOA = −7.5/+10.7 degrees) and 14.1 degrees (LOA = −6.6/+7.5). The authors concluded that because the smartphone app appears to be a reliable method for measuring knee ROM, it could be used as an alternative or additional method of knee joint measurement. It is easier to use than other photographic-based joint ROM assessments.

Reliability and Validity of Muscle Length Testing
Gajdosik  and  associates,19   in  a  study  of  30  healthy  males aged  18  to 40 years,  found that intrarater reliability intra- class correlation coefficients (ICCs) for the knee extension test were 0.86 when knee extension was performed actively and 0.90 when performed passively. Youdas and colleagues20  conducted a study to examine the effects of age and gender on hamstring muscle length (HML) as measured by passive straight leg raise and popliteal angle. The study consisted of 214 adults (108 women and 106 men) between the ages of 20 and 79 years. The trunk–thigh angle (PSLR) and the PA (thigh–leg angle) were estimated with a goniometer. Results showed  that  HML  differed  significantly  between  genders, with females demonstrating greater flexibility than their male counterparts. According to the data, the mean value of PSLR for women of 76.3 was closer to 80 degrees than the value for men of 68.5 degrees. The PSLR angle in men was signifi- cantly less than that in women.
Gnat and colleagues18  calculated correlation coefficients, standard errors of measurement, and smallest detectable dif- ference to evaluate reliability of the passive knee extension (PKE) test for length of the hamstring muscles. The results showed excellent reliability. The mean interrater ICC for the PKE test was 0.93.

Tibiofemoral and Patellofemoral Joints
Anatomy
The knee is composed of two distinct articulations enclosed within a single joint capsule: the tibiofemoral joint and the patellofemoral joint. At the tibiofemoral joint, the proximal joint surfaces are the convex medial and the lateral condyles of the distal femur (Fig. 9.1). Posteriorly and inferiorly, the


FIGURE 9.1  An anterior view of a right knee showing the tibiofemoral joint.

longer medial condyle is separated from the lateral condyle by a deep groove called the intercondylar notch. Anteriorly, the condyles are separated by a shallow area of bone called the femoral patellar surface. The distal articulating surfaces are the two shallow concave medial and lateral condyles on the proximal end of the tibia. Two bony spines called the intercondylar tubercles separate the medial condyle from the lateral condyle. Two joint discs called menisci are attached to the articulating surfaces on the tibial condyles (Fig. 9.2). At the patellofemoral joint, the articulating surfaces are the pos- terior surface of the patella and the femoral patellar surface (Fig. 9.3).
The joint capsule that encloses bothjoints is large, loose, and reinforced by tendons and expansions from the surround- ing muscles and ligaments. The quadriceps tendon, patellar ligament, and expansions from the extensor muscles provide anterior stability (see Fig. 9.3). Osteokinematics
The tibiofemoral joint is a double condyloidjoint with 2 degrees of freedom.  Flexion–extension  occurs  in  the  sagittal  plane around a medial–lateral axis; rotation occurs in the transverse plane around a vertical (longitudinal) axis.1 The incongruence and asymmetry of the tibiofemoral joint surfaces combined with muscle activity and ligamentous restraints produce an automatic rotation. This automatic rotation is involuntary and occurs primarily toward the end of extension when motion stops on the shorter lateral femoral condyle but continues on the longer medial condylar surface. During the last portion of active extension range of motion (ROM) automatic rotation produces what is referred to as either the screw-home mecha- nism, or “locking,” of the knee. For example, during non– weight-bearing active knee extension with the tibia moving on  the  femur,  the  tibia  laterally  rotates  during  the  last 10 to 15 degrees of extension to lock the knee.2 Therefore, in the fully extended position of the knee, the tibia is laterally rotated in relation to the femur. To unlock the knee, either the tibia has to rotate medially or the femur has to rotate laterally to unlock the knee. This rotation is not under voluntary con- trol and should not be confused with the voluntary rotation movement possible at the joint when the knee is ﬂexed.
Passive ROM in ﬂexion is generally considered to be between 130 and 140 degrees. The range of extension beyond 0 degrees is about 5 to 10 degrees in young children, whereas
0 degrees is considered to be within normal limits for adults.3

Arthrokinematics
In non–weight-bearing active motion, the concave tibialartic- ulating surfaces slide on the convex femoral condyles in the same direction as the movement of the shaft of the tibia. The tibial condyles slide posteriorly on the femoral condyles dur- ing ﬂexion, and the tibial condyles slide anteriorly on the femoral condyles during extension.
The incongruence of the tibiofemoral joint and the fact that the femoral articulating surfaces are larger than the tibial articulating surfaces dictate that when the femoral condyles are moving on the tibial condyles (in a weight-bearing situa- tion) the femoral condyles must roll and slide to remain on the tibia.  In weight-bearing ﬂexion,  the femoral  condyles roll posteriorly and slide anteriorly. The menisci follow the roll of the condyles by distorting posteriorly in ﬂexion. In exten- sion, the femoral condyles roll anteriorly and slide posteriorly.1  In the last portion of extension, motion stops at the lateral femoral condyle, but sliding continues on the medial femoral condyleto produce locking of the knee.
The patella slides superiorly in extension and inferiorly in ﬂexion. Some patellar rotation and tilting accompany the sliding during ﬂexion and extension. 1
Capsular Pattern
The capsular pattern at the knee is characterized by a smaller limitation of extension than of ﬂexion and no restriction of rotations.4,5  Fritz  and associates6  found that patients with a capsular pattern, deﬁned as aratio of extension loss to ﬂexion loss between 0.03 and 0.50, were 3.2 times more likely to have arthritis or arthroses of the knee. Hayes reported a mean ratio of extension loss to ﬂexion loss of 0.40 in a study of 79 patients with osteoarthritis.7,8

Beighton,  Solomon,   and  Soskolne23   defined  more  than 10 degrees of knee extension beyond 0 as hyperextension and included this criterion in a study of joint laxity in 1081 males and females. Females in the study had more joint lax- ity than males at any age.  Loudon,  Goist,  and Loudon31  operationally defined knee hyperextension (genu recurva- tum) as more than 5 degrees of extension beyond the 0 posi- tion. Clinically, the authors had observed that not only was hyperextension more common in females than males, but that  the  condition  might  be  associated  with  functional deficits in muscle strength, instability, and poor propriocep- tive  control   of  terminal   knee   extension.   The  authors cautioned that the female athlete with hyperextended knees maybe at risk for anterior cruciate ligament injury. Hall and colleagues32 found that  10 female patients diagnosed with hypermobility syndrome had alterations in proprioceptive acuity  at  the  knee  compared  with  an  age-matched  and gender-matched control group.
James and Parker33 studied knee ﬂexion ROM in 80 men and women who ranged in age from 70 years to older than 85 years. Women in this group had greater ROM in both ac- tive and passive knee ﬂexion than men. Overall knee ﬂexion values were lower than expected for both genders, possibly owing to the fact that the subjects were measured in the prone

Intrasessional absolute differences ranged from 0 to 2.7 degrees in the control group and 0 to 2.4 degrees in the cerebral palsy (CP) group. Intrases- sional ICCs were good in the control group (ICC  = 0.79 to 0.87) and excellent in the CP group (ICC = 0.97 to 0.99). Inter- sessional ICCs were lower for both the control and CP group, but only the control group had unacceptable ICCs (0.34 to 0.67) compared to an ICC  of 0.89 to 0.92 for the CP group. Cleffken and associates34conducted a study to determine both intratester and intertester reproducibility for measurements of active and passive knee ﬂexion and extension in 42 healthy volunteers. Each motion was measured by two testers three times in four measurements sessions. Measurements of pas- sive  maximum ﬂexion of the  knee  resulted in a smaller detectable difference (SDD = 0 ± 6.4 degrees) than active knee ﬂexion (SDD = 0 ± 7.4 degrees) for intertester compar- isons. Intratester reliability showed better reproducibility with SDDs reduced by 0.4 to 1.9 degrees over intertester values.

Piriyaprasarth  and  colleagues61     assessed   intratester   and intertester reliability of measurements using a ﬂexible electro- goniometer of two different ﬁxed ﬂexion angles  (45  and 75 degrees) in sitting, supine, and standing positions Thirty- seven healthy volunteers (mean age 31 years) participated in the intratester study, and 35 healthy volunteers (mean age 30 years) participated in the intertester reliability study. Ten repetitions of joint angles were taken by two testers. Intra- tester reliability of measurements ranged from fair for supine (ICC = 0.75 to 0.76), good in sitting (ICC = 0.86 to 0.87), to very good in standing (ICC = 0.87 to 0.88). Intertester relia- bility was poor to fair for supine (ICC = 0.58 to 0.71), poor to fair for sitting (ICC = 0.68 to 0.79), and poor to good for standing (ICC = 0.57 to 0.80). The sitting position had larger ICCs and lower standard errors of measurement (SEMs) for both intratester and intertester reliability compared to the supine position. One drawback of the study was that only angles less than 90  degrees  were  measured.  The  SEM  was  less  than 1.7 degrees when the same tester repeated the measurements.

Enwemeka52   compared the measurements  of six knee joint positions (0, 15, 30, 45, 60, and 90 degrees) taken with a UG  with bone angle measurements provided by radio- graphs. The measurements were taken on 10 healthy adult volunteers  (four  women  and  six  men)   between  21  and 35 years of age. The mean differences ranged from 0.52 to 3.81 degrees between goniometric and radiographic measure- ments taken between 30 and 90 degrees of ﬂexion. However, mean differences were higher (4.59 degrees) between gonio- metric and radiographic measurements of the smaller angles between 0 and 15 degrees.
Ersoz  and  Ergun28    used  a  UG  with  25-cm  arms  and 1-degree increments to measure the ROM in both knees of 20 patients with bilateral knee osteoarthritis. Radiographs were taken of tibiofemoral, lateral tibiofemoral,  and patellofemoral compartments of the same knees. The authors found a clear relationship  between  knee  ROM  measurements  of  ﬂexion,

extension,  and medial  and lateral rotation taken with a UG and radiographs. For example, limitations in internal rotation ROM provided a prediction of advanced disease in the lateral knee compartment. The authors concluded that measurements ofjoint ROM were helpful in the determination of the compart- mentor compartments that were affected by the disease process.
Brousseau and associates60 measured active knee ﬂexion in two positions in 60 healthy university students (44 females and 16 males) with a mean age of 21 years. Two trained testers alternately used either a universal  (UG) or a pendulum (PG) goniometer for the measurements. Eight measurements were taken with the knee ﬂexed in the supine position and eight with the knee in the ﬁrst 20 degrees of ﬂexion in the supine position. A radiograph was taken of each subject in each knee position. Criterion validity was determined by calculating Pearson prod- uct moment correlation coefﬁcients between each goniometric and radiologic measurement. Results showed that both the PGs and UGs had higher validity when measuring the larger ﬁxed knee ﬂexion angle compared to the smaller angle when using radiographs as the gold standard.
Rheault  and  coworkers50     investigated  the  concurrent validity of a UG and an inclinometer for measurements of active knee ﬂexion. Each instrument had good validity,  but instruments could not be used interchangeably.
